bull_thesis:
OR Royalties owns one of the cleanest business models in mining and is priced today as if it were an ordinary miner. It holds contractual claims - net smelter return royalties (a fixed percentage of a mine's revenue) and streams (the right to buy metal at a fixed low price) - on 23 to 24 paying mines run by other people. It pays none of the mining costs, funds none of the capital spending, and absorbs none of the cost inflation that has eaten operating miners' margins through this cycle. The proof is a cash margin of 96.8% in the second quarter of 2026, essentially unchanged from 96.7% in 2025 and from every quarter before it. Wheaton Precious Metals, the sector benchmark, does not match it.

The growth is already bought and paid for, which is rare. Management guided 80,000 to 90,000 gold-equivalent ounces for 2026 and 120,000 to 135,000 for 2030 - roughly 50% more ounces - and the assets that deliver it are already owned: the Namdini mine in Ghana (the royalty consolidated to a full 2% in January 2026 for up to $103.5 million), Buenaventura's San Gabriel mine in Peru (a 1.5% royalty inside the $115 million Gold Fields portfolio bought in February 2026), Ramelius's Dalgaranga in Western Australia (first ore delivered to the Mt Magnet plant in February 2026), and the expanded Spring Valley royalties in Nevada (the $168 million Terraco acquisition, closed in April 2026). Getting from here to 2030 does not require another cheque. As the chief executive put it in February 2026, the company has "the luxury of walking away from bad deals to wait for the right ones."

The asset quality is genuinely differentiated. Just under 75% of 2025 ounces came from Canada, the United States and Australia, and closer to 90% including Chile - the best jurisdictional mix in the peer group, and the reason this book should not carry the expropriation discount applied to royalties on West African or Andean-frontier ounces. The reserve lives behind the contracts are long: management describes underwriting "assets with 15- to 25-year mine lives," and the cornerstone, Agnico Eagle's Canadian Malartic, has an underground mine at Odyssey that Agnico still expects to carry the complex to a million ounces a year in the early 2030s.

The financial record corroborates the story rather than contradicting it. Net debt of just under $35 million at the end of 2024 was paid down to $10 million by the first quarter of 2025, to net cash by the second, and to zero debt by the third - each step delivered on the call it was promised. Operating cash flow set a record $245.6 million in 2025 and rose 56% year over year in the first quarter of 2026. Cash flow per share has risen eight years running. The dividend has been paid 46 consecutive quarters and was raised 20% in 2025 and 18.2% in May 2026, to $0.065 a quarter, which is roughly 20% to 25% of operating cash flow - covered several times over.

What has to hold for this to work. First, gold needs to hold somewhere near today's $4,154 an ounce rather than round-trip to its 12-month low of $3,353; a royalty converts price into cash almost one-for-one, so this is the dominant variable. Second, Agnico Eagle needs to restart the Barnat open pit on the schedule it published - remediation complete in the third quarter of 2026, mining resuming in the fourth. Third, Capstone's Mantos Blancos silver grades need to stop disappointing, which management has prudently guided flat to 2030 rather than assumed away. If those hold, a book generating roughly $336 million of cash earnings in 2027 on today's metal prices, growing to 120,000-plus ounces by 2030, deserves the 20-to-21-times multiple its senior peers carry, and the shares are worth materially more than $31.19.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not require the business to be bad. It requires only that the price already reflects the business, that the cornerstone asset has a two-year hole in it, and that management spent the balance sheet at the top of the cycle. All three are true today.

Start with the cornerstone, because it is the largest royalty in the book by a wide margin. On 1 July 2026 a rock mass movement occurred along the north wall of the Barnat open pit at Canadian Malartic. Agnico Eagle suspended mining, and said the same week it expects to lose 60,000 to 80,000 ounces of gold in the second half of 2026 and up to approximately 150,000 ounces a year in both 2027 and 2028. At OR's 5% Barnat royalty that is roughly 3,000 to 4,000 ounces this year and up to 7,500 ounces a year in 2027 and 2028 - about 8% of a mid-range year, removed from precisely the two years that were supposed to bridge to the 2030 target. Worse for a royalty holder specifically: while the pit is shut the mill is being fed low-grade stockpile, and a net smelter return royalty is paid on the revenue the mine actually earns, so low-grade feed is a direct revenue cut, not a timing difference. OR's response, published the same day, was that its "2026 gold equivalent ounce delivery guidance range, as well as its 5-year outlook, remain unchanged." The 2026 claim survives only at the bottom of the 80,000-to-90,000 range: the first half delivered 43,497 ounces, and a flat second half less the Barnat drag lands around 81,000 to 82,000. The five-year claim does not survive the arithmetic in the middle years at all.

Second, the capital discipline that was the entire investment case in 2025 has been reversed. Management spent the February 2026 call celebrating restraint - "OR Royalties transacted on only just $25 million in royalty and stream acquisitions" while the sector did $9.3 billion - and then committed $438.5 million across four transactions in the following weeks, plus up to $96 million to Canadian Copper, a Canadian Securities Exchange-listed base-metals developer, in April. Those cheques were written with gold between roughly $4,500 and $5,600 an ounce. Gold is $4,154 today; silver has fallen from a 12-month high of $121 to $60. Buying a royalty is buying a claim on a metal price, and these were bought near the high. The balance-sheet consequence is already visible: $90.6 million of net cash at 31 March 2026 became $139.4 million of net debt at 30 June - a $230 million swing in one quarter, with the Terraco purchase funded by drawing the revolving credit facility. Any valuation that still adds back net cash, including the screener bundle's own instruction to do so, is a quarter and a sign out of date.

Third, the shares are not cheap once the earnings figure is cleaned. The trailing enterprise-value-to-earnings multiple of 15.7 times flatters, because trailing earnings include non-cash gains - most visibly a $54 million revaluation of the Osisko Development stake in the third quarter of 2025 - which is why the implied margin exceeds 100%. On a cash basis the multiple is about 20 times, the same as Franco-Nevada at 20.6 and Wheaton at 21.0, and above Royal Gold at 17.5 and Triple Flag at 15.1. OR has lower returns than Wheaton (13.9% return on invested capital against 18.1%), a smaller and more concentrated asset base, and thinner trading liquidity at roughly $10 million a day. There is no discount here to harvest.

Fourth, the downside is arithmetic, and the torque cuts both ways. A 10% move in the metal swings cash earnings about 9.7% - roughly $33 million on a $336 million base - in either direction. Gold falling from $4,154 to its 12-month low of $3,400 is an 18% move, worth about $59 million of lost cash earnings, and royalty multiples compress as the metal falls rather than holding. Take volumes to 85,000 ounces (the Barnat hole offsetting the ramp-ups), take the multiple to 15.5 times, and the equity is worth about $20 a share - roughly a third below today's price. There is no structural floor to catch it: no deal terms, no tender, and the net-cash cushion has been spent.

What would confirm the bear. Gold breaking below roughly $3,800 an ounce. A slip in the Barnat remediation timetable past the fourth quarter of 2026. A 2027 guidance range published in February 2027 that is flat or down against 2026 - which would concede the two-year hole management has so far declined to acknowledge. Or a fifth acquisition financed with equity rather than the revolver, which would tell you the balance sheet is no longer the strategic advantage it was described as.

What holds us back is three specific things, and the first two are new since June.

The cornerstone has a hole in it. On 1 July 2026 the Barnat open pit at Canadian Malartic - the source of the largest royalty in the book - was suspended after a wall movement. Agnico Eagle expects to lose 60,000 to 80,000 ounces in the second half of 2026 and up to approximately 150,000 ounces a year in both 2027 and 2028, which at a 5% royalty is up to 7,500 ounces a year, about 8% of a mid-range year, removed from exactly the years that bridge to 2030. When a company answers a published operator disclosure with a reassurance rather than a number, that is the thing to test first, and the second-quarter call in the coming days is where it gets tested.

The capital discipline that was the 2025 investment case has reversed. Management spent the February 2026 call celebrating $25 million of restraint against a $9.3 billion sector, then committed $438.5 million across four deals in the following weeks and up to $96 million more to a Canadian Securities Exchange-listed copper developer in April - with gold between roughly $4,500 and $5,600 an ounce, against $4,154 today. The screener bundle's instruction to add back $91 million of net cash is now a quarter and a sign out of date, and any valuation carrying it is overstated by about $1.20 a share. The buyback compounds the point: C$50.8 million in 2025 and C$17.7 million in the first quarter of 2026, the quarter the Toronto shares peaked at C$65.31, versus 26,000 shares when the stock was near $23 in 2024. This board buys high.

And the shares are not actually cheap. The screen's 15.7 times trailing earnings is an artefact: OR's reported earnings include non-cash gains, most visibly a $54 million Osisko Development revaluation in the third quarter of 2025, which is why the implied margin exceeds 100%. Cleaned to cash, the multiple is about 20 to 21 times - parity with Franco-Nevada at 20.6 and Wheaton at 21.0, and a premium to Royal Gold at 17.5 and Triple Flag at 15.1 - on lower returns than Wheaton and a more concentrated book. Reconciling the two sum-of-the-parts cases gives a base fair value near $35 a share, built almost entirely (95%) from the producing royalty book at a 2027 run-rate of 92,000 ounces on today's spot metals, at 19 times cash earnings, plus small credits for undeveloped royalties and the equity portfolio, less the new net debt. Against $31.19 that is roughly 12% of upside. The adverse case, with gold back at its 12-month low of $3,400 and multiples compressing, is about $20 - roughly a third lower - and nothing structural catches it, because there is no deal, no tender and no net cash any more.

So the timing call and the value call land in the same place for different reasons, and both land at neutral. On timing, the cornerstone is shut, the metal regime is neutral at best with gold below its 200-day average, the balance sheet just flipped, and results print within days - that argues for waiting. On pure valuation and forensic quality, ignoring all of that: clean books, a wide moat, a credible management record, and a 12% discount to fair value - a good business, an unremarkable price. Neither justifies a seat today.

The level we are waiting for is $27, near the 12-month low of $27.54, which would put the shares at roughly 15 times our base-case cash earnings and open a genuine margin of safety toward $35. The developments that would bring the entry forward without that price are a Barnat restart confirmed on schedule in the fourth quarter of 2026, or a second-quarter call in which management revises the 2027-2028 outlook honestly rather than repeating that nothing has changed. The development that would take this off the list entirely is a fifth acquisition financed with equity - which would say the balance sheet is no longer the advantage this company has spent two years telling us it is.
interrogator_dossier:
# OR Royalties Inc. (NYSE/TSX: OR) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared 4 August 2026. Price used throughout: US$31.19 on the New York listing (the company reports in US dollars and the New York and Toronto listings share the ticker "OR"; all figures below are US dollars unless a Canadian-dollar amount is explicitly marked).*

OR Royalties is not a miner. It owns royalty and streaming contracts — legal claims that entitle it to a fixed slice of the gold and silver that other companies dig out of the ground, without paying any of the mining costs. It has 23 to 24 paying assets, its single biggest being a 3% to 5% net smelter return royalty (a percentage of the revenue a mine earns from selling its metal) on Agnico Eagle's Canadian Malartic complex in Quebec.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Across the six calls in evidence — February 2025 through February 2026 — the story moved through three distinct chapters, and the company was honest about each transition as it happened.

**Chapter one, "fix the balance sheet" (February 2025 to August 2025).** The opening call was a deleveraging story. Management had paid down almost $85 million of a revolving credit facility during 2024 and finished the year with $59 million of cash against just under $35 million of net debt. By the first quarter of 2025 net debt was "just over $10 million"; by the second quarter the company was in net cash "for the first time in several years"; by the third quarter it was, in the chief executive's words, "in a debt-free position for the first time in over 10 years." Three consecutive calls each delivered exactly the next step management had promised on the prior one. That is the single most credible sequence in the file.

**Chapter two, "discipline as a virtue" (August 2025 to February 2026).** As precious-metal prices ran, the emphasis shifted from repairing the balance sheet to refusing to spend it. Jason Attew, the chief executive, told the November 2025 call he continued "to espouse an internal culture of capital allocation discipline, where returns on new transactions must exceed our internal hurdle rates at what we believe internally to be more realistic commodity pricing scenarios." The February 2026 call turned that into a boast: the company transacted on "only just $25 million in royalty and stream acquisitions" in 2025, against more than $9.3 billion of deals across the sector. The phrase used was "we prioritize value over volume," and the justification offered was structural: "Because our near-term growth is already secured and fully funded, we possess a strategic advantage many peers lack, the luxury of walking away from bad deals."

**Chapter three, "spend it all" (January 2026 onward).** This chapter is not in the transcripts — it is in the press releases, and it inverts chapter two. In a single quarter the company committed $438.5 million: an additional 1.0% royalty on the Namdini mine in Ghana for up to $103.5 million (29 January), a portfolio of eight royalties bought from Gold Fields for $115 million, anchored by a 1.5% royalty on Buenaventura's San Gabriel mine in Peru (18 February), and the Terraco Gold subsidiary holding royalties over the Spring Valley project in Nevada for $168 million cash (24 February). A fourth commitment followed on 14 April 2026: up to $96 million of project financing into Canadian Copper Inc., a Canadian Securities Exchange-listed developer of a base-metals complex in New Brunswick.

The growth drivers quietly dropped along the way are worth naming. Diamonds — the Renard mine — disappeared entirely between 2024 and 2025. Direct equity ownership of Osisko Development, the affiliated developer, was deliberately diluted from close to 50% down to 14.3% over 2024 and 2025, which management framed as a positive ("we were no longer going to be funding the Osisko Development, Cariboo through equity placements"). The growth drivers added are copper — first through the CSA mine stream, now through Canadian Copper — from a management that has said repeatedly and in plain terms, "we are a precious metal vehicle."

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Stable, with a distinct hardening into 2026.**

*February 2025 — cautiously optimistic, with a hedge.* "Not only does our long-term growth trajectory still spell great things coming for Osisko five years out… However, the slope of that growth is likely less steep than we previously anticipated." That volunteered "however" is a good sign; it is a management team telling you the bad half before an analyst asks.

*May 2025 — confident, promotional at the margins.* The name change to OR Royalties was announced with a flourish: "Commodity prices are elevated, our assets are performing well, the balance sheet is strong, and we're just getting started." No analyst asked a single question on that call — a fact worth noting in itself.

*August 2025 — specific and measured.* Management quantified its own shortfall unprompted: "approximately 1,200 GEOs that were not realized compared to our internal budget due to the higher gold/silver ratio." Volunteering a miss of that size, in that detail, is the behaviour of a team that expects to be checked.

*November 2025 — defensive in the good sense.* The language turned toward what the company would not do: "internal red lines regarding structural security and contract terms," "we have the fortunate luxury to be able to walk away." Attew gave Tanya Jakusconek of Scotiabank an unusually concrete answer on the cost of capital — "approximately, it's about 4.5% in terms of our cost of capital or cost of debt" — and named a real precedent, the mid-teens internal rate of return on the Cascabel transaction.

*February 2026 — the most promotional call in the file.* "The enviable triple crown of record annual revenues… record operating cash flow… and record earnings." "For us, 2025 prove that boring is good." A "50% growth trajectory through to 2030." This was delivered two days before the shares set a 12-month high on the Toronto listing at C$65.31.

The shift is not from offence to defence. It is from a repair story told plainly to a growth story told with more adjectives, arriving exactly at the top of the price cycle.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**High, with one live exception.**

The delivery record is genuinely good and covers three separate promise types.

*Volume guidance.* 2024: 80,740 ounces against 77,000–83,000, slightly above the midpoint of a range that had itself been revised down during the year. 2025: 80,775 against 80,000–88,000 — inside, at the bottom on the raw number, mid-range once adjusted for the gold-to-silver ratio actually realised versus the 83-to-1 assumed. Management flagged that ratio drag twice before the year ended, in August and again in November, rather than explaining it after the fact. That is the opposite of sandbagging: they told you the number would look soft and why, and it did.

*Balance-sheet guidance.* Every step promised was delivered on the call it was promised for. See section 2.

*Dividend guidance.* In February 2025 management said that come May "there should be a recommendation by this management team to our Board to increase our dividend." The board approved a 20% increase in May 2025. In February 2026 management pre-announced the same intention for the first quarter results; an 18.2% increase to $0.065 per share followed on 6 May 2026. Forty-six consecutive quarterly dividends, and inclusion in the Canadian dividend-aristocrat index in January 2026.

*The exception.* The 2030 outlook published in February 2026 — 120,000 to 135,000 ounces — landed below what analysts expected. Derick Ma of TD said so directly: "Guidance came in below expectations and at least certainly below my estimates." That is the first guidance event in the file that disappointed, and it came after a year of "50% growth" messaging. Reaffirming that same outlook as "unchanged" on 2 July, hours after the operator of the cornerstone asset published a two-year production hole, is the one place where the credibility record is exposed.

**Reliability score: High**, downgraded from the top mark solely by the 2 July reaffirmation.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Analysts pushed on three things, repeatedly, across every call.

**Deal size, and the refusal to narrow it.** Tanya Jakusconek of Scotiabank asked the same question four times across four calls and got a wider answer each time. February 2025: "$50 million and $500 million." August 2025: "somewhere around USD 35 million all the way up to close to the USD $1 billion." November 2025: her own words were "you can drive a truck through that," and the answer came back to "$50 million and $500 million." February 2026: "$100 million to $200 million, but we're also seeing opportunities from $750 million all the way up to $1 billion." A range that will not converge over a full year is a range that is not a plan. It is also the range within which they subsequently spent $438.5 million in a single quarter.

**The hurdle rate.** Jakusconek pressed in November 2025 for the actual internal rate of return required. The answer began with a deflection — "maybe we can take this conversation offline" — before landing on a genuine number (a spread over roughly 4.5%, with a mid-teens precedent). Partial credit: he did eventually answer, but the reflex was to move it off the record.

**Mantos Blancos silver grades.** This came up on five of six calls and never resolved. February 2025: throughput fixed, "Capstone has officially turned the corner." May 2025: "lower silver grades at the front of the year," grades expected to "trend back upwards." August 2025: grades still low, and the Phase 2 feasibility study slipped from the fourth quarter of 2025 into 2026. November 2025: grades improved, but for "approximately a month's worth." February 2026: "we've continued to see some quarterly variability of the processed silver grades," and 2026 was guided flat. Brian MacArthur of Raymond James put the unspoken part on the record in February 2026: "just given the reconciliation that we've been seeing or not seeing." Reconciliation is the comparison between the grade a geological model predicts and the grade the mill actually recovers. When it persistently disappoints, the model is wrong. Management has guided this asset flat to 2030 rather than fix the estimate — which is prudent, but also means a stream carrying a large share of revenue is one the operator cannot yet predict.

**What nobody asked about that mattered.** No analyst in the file pressed on wall stability or geotechnical risk at Barnat, the pit that produces the ounces underpinning the largest royalty. That risk was not hidden — Agnico later disclosed the failed area "had been previously identified as having weaker geological structures within the north wall" and was under enhanced monitoring — but it was never a topic on an OR call.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- *The discipline whipsaw (January to April 2026).* A company that spent the February 2026 call celebrating $25 million of restraint committed $438.5 million over the following weeks, plus up to $96 million more in April. The deals were struck while gold traded between roughly $4,500 and $5,600 an ounce, the top of its range; gold is $4,154 today, and silver has fallen from a 12-month high of $121 to $60. Buying royalties is buying a claim on a metal price; buying them at the top is the sector's oldest mistake.
- *Net cash to net debt in one quarter (31 March to 30 June 2026).* From $90.6 million of net cash to $139.4 million of net debt, a $230 million reversal. The screener bundle's instruction to treat net cash of $91 million as a valuation add-back is now wrong by a quarter and by a sign.
- *Buying back stock into strength, not weakness.* C$50.8 million repurchased across 2025 and a further C$17.7 million (US$12.9 million) in the first quarter of 2026 — the quarter in which the Toronto shares set a 12-month high of C$65.31 on 27 February. In 2024, by contrast, when the shares were "slightly below $23" after a disappointment, the company bought "a whopping 26,000 shares," which Attew himself conceded "wasn't much." The buyback has been countercyclical in exactly the wrong direction.
- *Drift from the stated mandate.* "We are a precious metal vehicle. We'll continue to be a precious metal vehicle" (February 2025). In April 2026 the company committed up to $96 million to a base-metals developer listed on the Canadian Securities Exchange.
- *"Outlook unchanged" on 2 July 2026.* Discussed above. It is one sentence, but it is the sentence a director should test first.

**Green flags**

- *The cash margin is real and it is the best in its peer group.* 96.7% for 2025, 96.8% in the second quarter of 2026, and it has not moved in either direction across the file. This is what a royalty is supposed to look like and many do not.
- *Every balance-sheet promise was kept, in order, on time.* Three consecutive calls, three delivered steps to debt-free.
- *Jurisdiction quality is genuinely differentiated.* Just under 75% of 2025 ounces came from Canada, the United States and Australia, closer to 90% including Chile. In a sector where the cheapest assets are cheap for reasons that show up as expropriation risk, this is a durable advantage, and it survived the 2026 buying spree (San Gabriel adds Peru; Spring Valley adds Nevada).
- *Management volunteers its own shortfalls.* The 1,200-ounce ratio miss in August 2025 and the "slope of that growth is likely less steep" hedge in February 2025 were both unprompted.
- *Growth is bought and paid for.* Whatever one thinks of the price, Namdini, San Gabriel, Dalgaranga and Spring Valley are owned. The path from 80,000–90,000 ounces this year to 120,000–135,000 in 2030 does not require another cheque.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**"Producing" quietly became "producing and/or paying."** In February 2025 management drew the distinction itself: 21 producing assets, or 20 "if Namdini is excluded," because a mine can pour gold months before a royalty holder sees a payment. Namdini poured first gold in November 2024 and OR's first payment — 130 ounces — arrived in the second quarter of 2025. The asset-count metric is therefore softer than it sounds, and it has since climbed to 23 and then 24 partly by counting assets in ramp-up. San Gabriel and Dalgaranga are both described as "ramping up this year and the next and growing into a material contributor from 2028 onwards." The count is up; the ounces from those additions are two years out.

**The equity portfolio is a shrinking, unhedged asset.** Long-term investments stood at $210.5 million at 31 March 2026. The largest identified piece is roughly 14.3% of Osisko Development, whose shares trade at $2.28 today against a 12-month high of $4.795 — down more than half. Whatever that line was worth at the March balance-sheet date, it is worth materially less now, and none of it produces cash.

**Elliott Management appeared and then went quiet.** Asked in August 2025, Attew confirmed "the last public disclosure that we see is Elliott owns 2.2 million OR Royalties shares" — roughly 1.2% of the company — and no further filing has surfaced. Two board seats changed hands in early 2026 (Kevin Thomson appointed and William Murray John resigned on 30 January; Patrick Godin appointed on 23 March). That is a board refresh, not visibly a proxy fight, and nothing in the file establishes a link.

**The copper option nobody is modelling.** Carey MacRury of Canaccord asked in November 2025 whether the buydown option on the CSA copper stream — the operator's right to buy back part of the stream — transferred when Harmony Gold took over from MAC Copper. It did, unchanged, exercisable from the fifth anniversary. A stream that can be repurchased by the operator is a shorter asset than one that cannot, and its value depends on a decision by a counterparty that has just told the market it will run CSA for the long term rather than push volumes.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Trajectory: Stable.**

The operating engine is exactly what management says it is. The margin is real, the guidance record is honest, the balance sheet was genuinely repaired, and the growth to 2030 is already owned rather than promised. Nothing in the file suggests a company misrepresenting itself.

What changed is not the business. It is the price paid for the next tranche of it. A management team that spent a full year explaining, persuasively, why it would not chase the market then wrote $438.5 million of cheques in one quarter at the top of the metal cycle, turned net cash into $139.4 million of net debt doing it, and bought back its own shares at a 12-month high while it was at it. None of those is fatal. Together they say that the discipline described in November 2025 was a description of conditions, not of temperament.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the gold price — the cornerstone. Canadian Malartic is the largest royalty in the book by a wide margin, and its open pit is shut. The operator says remediation finishes in the third quarter of 2026, mining resumes in the fourth, and up to 150,000 ounces a year are lost in both 2027 and 2028 regardless. The company's answer, published the same day, was that nothing changes. A director should price the two-year hole explicitly rather than accept the reassurance, and should treat the underground Odyssey mine — untouched by the incident, and the reason Agnico still expects a million ounces a year from the complex in the early 2030s — as the reason the long-dated value survives.

**Economic moat: wide, and stable.** The moat is contractual. A net smelter return royalty is an encumbrance registered against a mining title; it runs with the property, survives changes of operator (as Éléonore and CSA both demonstrated, passing to Dhilmar and Harmony Gold with no change to OR's terms), and cannot be competed away or inflated away, because OR pays none of the costs. The evidence supports width rather than erosion: return on equity of 19.9% and return on invested capital of 13.9% on the trailing year, both improved on 2024, with the cash margin flat at the top of its peer group. The honest limit on that moat is that it protects the assets already owned and does nothing to protect the price of the next one — royalty companies have no organic growth and must buy it against rivals with lower costs of capital, which is precisely where the 2026 spending sits.

**Secular threat: none.** There is no structural force eroding the terminal value of a claim on ounces in Quebec, Nevada and Western Australia. The reserve lives behind these contracts are long — management describes deploying capital "in assets with 15- to 25-year mine lives," and Odyssey alone underpins Canadian Malartic into the 2040s. The risk here is cyclical, not terminal: the metal price, and the price paid for new contracts. Cheapness in this name, where it exists, would be a cycle print rather than a melting base — but on today's numbers the cheapness is thinner than the screen suggests, because the reported earnings figure that makes it look cheap is inflated by non-cash gains.

There are three places where the market's working assumptions are demonstrably wrong, and only one of them favours the buyer.

First, and most concretely for this system: the automated data feeding this name is inflated by exactly a factor of two. Rio reports half-yearly rather than quarterly, so the trailing-twelve-month calculation summed four reporting periods — twenty-four months of trading. The four half-year figures reconcile to the bundle to the decimal: revenue of $31.02B, $30.65B, $27.10B and $26.86B sum to the stated $115.63B; free cash flow of $3.23B, $2.53B, $2.26B and $2.94B sum to the stated $10.97B; diluted earnings per share of $4.06, $3.31, $2.79 and $3.51 sum to the stated $13.67. Any process that sized this position off the raw feed would have bought a company it believed was half as expensive as it is.

Second, in the buyer's favour: the street is still pricing Rio as an iron ore company. That was true and is no longer. Copper, aluminium and lithium supplied more than half of first-half 2026 cash operating profit; copper alone earned $5.7B against iron ore's $6.8B and grew 84% while iron ore was flat. Rio's copper business, at net unit costs of 30–50 cents a pound and heading toward one million tonnes a year by 2030, is comparable in scale to Freeport-McMoRan, which the market values at 11.5 times cash profit against Rio's 7.2 for the whole group. The consensus price-target set is also unusually thin and stale — only one target printed in the last quarter (Richard Hatch at $113 on 30 July), against a $105.50 average that still carries Bernstein's $83.50 from April and $77 from March. A thin, stale target set is not a street-wide view, and both Berenberg and Goldman Sachs upgraded in the past week on precisely the parts-versus-whole argument.

Third, and against the buyer: the market is treating record commodity prices as a run-rate. Copper at about $6.65 a pound, aluminium realisations at $4,343 a tonne against a London Metal Exchange price near $3,416, and gold at about $4,152 an ounce are not normal conditions. The gold price is quietly doing real work — Rio's own explanation for cutting copper unit cost guidance on 15 July 2026 to 30–50 cents from 65–75 cents was 'higher than expected gold prices and productivity improvements'. A cost guide that moves with a metal price is not a cost position. The honest reconciliation of all three points is that Rio is a better company than the market thinks and a more expensive stock than the data said — and those two errors happen to cancel out to roughly fair value.
moderator_conclusion:
Rio Tinto is a better business than it was two years ago and a fully priced stock today. Both halves of that sentence matter.

The business case is strong and it is verified rather than asserted. First-half 2026 cash operating profit rose 28% to $14.8B and free cash flow 75% to $3.8B. The productivity programme promised $650M and banked $870M by June, with the year-end target nearly tripled to $1.8B. Copper, aluminium and lithium supplied more than half of group earnings for the first time — the diversification management has been promising since 2024 has actually landed. The cost position is first-quartile on both main legs and I have checked it against company-reported guidance rather than proxies: Pilbara iron ore at $23.5–25.0 a tonne against a seaborne price near $93, and copper net unit costs cut to 30–50 US cents a pound on 15 July 2026. The moat is a genuine scale-cost moat — sixty years of integrated Pilbara rail, port and power across eight billion tonnes shipped, Simandou's 1.5 billion tonnes at 65–66% iron with roughly twenty years of life, Gudai-Darri with more than forty. And the capital discipline is better than the sector's reputation deserves: Rio walked away from a Glencore merger on price, bought Arcadium near the lithium bottom, has refused to be a forced seller of its titanium dioxide and borates units, and carries net debt of $14.1B against about $28.6B of underlying annual cash profit.

Two things stop this being a buy.

The first is a data correction that changes the entire arithmetic. Every trailing figure in the automated bundle is a twenty-four-month sum, because Rio reports half-yearly and the calculation added four reporting periods. Verified trailing revenue is $61.7B, not $115.6B; free cash flow $5.76B, not $10.97B; diluted earnings per share $7.37, not $13.67. At $99.08 this is roughly 13.4 times earnings and a 3.6% free-cash-flow yield. The proxy said cheap; the company's own filings say fair.

The second is that the sum of the parts, built honestly on peer multiples, lands at $104 — about 5% above the $99.08 traded on 4 August 2026. The parts are worth more than the whole in kind but not by much in degree, and the structure that suppresses the gap is the dual-listed arrangement, which management has explicitly declined to unify after activist pressure. Against that 5% of base-case upside sits an adverse case at $62. The torque is not an assertion: a 10% adverse move across the basket costs roughly $5.5B of annual cash profit, about $20 a share of enterprise value, and I have checked the internal 25% figure bottom-up against Rio's own volumes at roughly 20%. Copper at $6.65 a pound, gold at $4,152 an ounce feeding the copper cost credit, and an aluminium realisation carrying roughly $900 a tonne of tariff-driven premium are all sitting at or near historic extremes. The shares have risen about 66% from their 52-week low and sit within 12% of the high, on a day the entire cohort rallied on falling oil.

So: wait for the wash-out, and here is the specific level and development rather than a vague hope for one. The level is **$78–82 a share** — roughly a 20% drawdown, which is what a single 10% adverse move in the commodity basket plus modest multiple compression produces, and which puts the base-case fair value of $104 at an honest 25%-plus discount. Bernstein's $83.50 target, published in April 2026, sits in that band. Alternatively, buy without the drawdown if the company supplies the missing ingredient: a completed $5B capital release with proceeds committed to a buyback at 0.65 times net asset value, confirmed at the February 2027 full-year result. Either the price comes to the parts or the company forces the parts onto the price. Until one of those happens, the asymmetry is roughly seven to one against, and no amount of asset quality fixes an entry price.

On the value case judged purely on price against the parts and on forensic quality, the score is a middling three rather than a buy: the forensics are clean, management's guidance record is strong, and the moat is wide and stable — but a 5% discount to fair value is not a margin of safety, and the discount that does exist is held open by a listing structure the board has refused to change.
interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic dossier — Rio Tinto Group (RIO)

**Prepared 4 August 2026. Price used throughout: $99.08 on the New York listing (the American depositary share, which represents one Rio Tinto plc ordinary share), up 3.3% on the day. The London line closed at 7,313 pence. Every figure below is in US dollars unless stated.**

Transcripts reviewed: 30 July 2024 (2024 half-year), 19 February 2025 (2024 full year), 19 February 2026 (2025 full year), 28 July 2026 (2026 half-year).

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Across four calls the story does not merely evolve — it changes owner and changes register.

**2024 (Jakob Stausholm, chief executive).** The framing is abstract and values-led: four objectives ("best operator, impeccable ESG, excel in development, social licence"). Growth is asserted rather than counted — "we are profitable, and we are growing… this is stable, reliable growth." The hard numbers are modest: half-year underlying earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA — a rough measure of cash operating profit) of $12.1B, up 3%; free cash flow of $2.8B; net debt of $5.1B. The single concrete event is the July 2024 sanctioning of Simandou, the Guinean iron ore project, described as "the largest greenfield mining and infrastructure project in the world."

**Early 2025.** The word that arrives is *diversification*: "the diversification towards copper, aluminium and lithium is happening at pace." Full-year EBITDA of $23.3B was down 2% on an 11% lower iron ore price, and management leans hard on the offset from copper and aluminium. Capital spending steps up to $9.5B and net debt drifts to $5.5B. The Arcadium lithium acquisition is folded in as evidence the portfolio is being reshaped.

**February 2026 — the handover.** Simon Trott presents his first full-year result and the vocabulary is replaced wholesale. Out go the four objectives; in comes "stronger, sharper and simpler," a "management operating system," and a running productivity tally. Full-year EBITDA rises 9% to $25.4B on 8% copper-equivalent production growth and a 5% cut in copper-equivalent unit costs. Two genuinely new commitments appear: $5B to $10B of cash proceeds from selling non-core assets, and 85% of the exploration budget redirected to copper. He also discloses, unprompted, that Rio held merger discussions with Glencore and walked away: "strategic rationales don't pay the grocery bills."

**July 2026 — the evidence arrives.** Half-year EBITDA of $14.8B, up 28%; free cash flow of $3.8B, up 75%; an interim dividend of $3.4B (211.0 US cents per share), up 43%. Copper, aluminium and lithium together supply more than half of group EBITDA for the first time. The productivity programme, promised at $650M, has banked $870M by June, and the year-end target is nearly tripled to $1.8B.

**The quiet drop.** Iron ore growth has left the story. In July 2024 management pointed to "medium-term guidance of 345 to 360" million tonnes from the Pilbara, backed by four replacement mines. The 2026 guidance is 323–338 million tonnes from the Pilbara, with the group total of 343–366 million tonnes made up by Simandou and the Canadian operation. The Pilbara growth promise was not withdrawn loudly; it was diluted into a group number. Simandou is now doing work that four Australian replacement mines were once meant to do.

---

## 2. Claims versus the financials

An important correction first, because it governs everything below. **The deterministic metrics bundle supplied with this name is wrong by exactly a factor of two, and it is wrong in the flattering direction.** Rio reports twice a year, not quarterly, so the automated "trailing twelve months" calculation summed four reporting periods — which is twenty-four months of trading, not twelve.

| Bundle field | Bundle value | Verified true trailing twelve months | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $115.63B | **$61.67B** | $30.65B (H2 2025) + $31.02B (H1 2026) |
| EBITDA | $41.85B | **$23.35B** statutory / ~$28.6B underlying | FMP statements + company releases |
| Free cash flow | $10.97B | **$5.76B** | $2.53B + $3.23B |
| Diluted earnings per share | $13.67 | **$7.37** | $3.31 + $4.06 |

The four half-year figures sum to the bundle values to the decimal, so this is arithmetic, not estimation. The practical consequence: at $99.08 the shares trade on roughly **13.4 times trailing earnings and a 3.6% free-cash-flow yield**, not the 7.2 times and 6.8% the bundle implies. Anyone sizing this position off the raw bundle is looking at a company half as expensive as the real one.

With that fixed, management's claims test well.

| Management claim | Where | Verdict against the numbers |
|---|---|---|
| "28 per cent increase in underlying EBITDA and a 75 per cent rise in free cash flow" | Jul 2026 | **Confirmed.** $14.8B versus $11.6B; $3.8B versus $2.2B on the company's definition. The statutory cash-flow statement shows free cash flow of $3.23B against $2.26B (+43%); the gap is definitional, and management should be read as using its own measure. |
| Productivity of $650M by end-Q1 2026 | Feb 2026 | **Over-delivered.** $870M banked by 30 June, and the year-end run-rate target raised to $1.8B. |
| "Copper equivalent production up 3 per cent" in the half | Jul 2026 | **Confirmed** by the 14 July production release. |
| "One of the lowest cost positions in the sector" in copper | Jul 2026 | **Confirmed but qualified.** On 15 July 2026 the company cut its copper net unit cost guidance to 30–50 US cents per pound from 65–75 cents. Rio's own explanation is "higher than expected gold prices and productivity improvements." Gold is at roughly $4,152 an ounce. A large slice of that cost improvement is a by-product credit — a gold-price artifact wearing a cost-performance costume. Management discloses the reason honestly; the reader must simply not capitalise it as permanent. |
| Pilbara unit costs of $23 a tonne, guided about 3% higher | Feb 2025 | **Held, then drifted.** 2026 guidance is $23.5–25.0 a tonne, with roughly $0.80 a tonne of the first-half increase attributed to diesel moving from about $85 to about $140 a barrel. Brent is back to about $79 as of 4 August 2026, so this headwind is now reversing. |
| Balance sheet "in good shape," gearing 18% | Feb/Jul 2026 | **Confirmed.** Net debt of $14.1B (company-reported at 30 June 2026, down $0.3B in the half) against roughly $28.6B of underlying EBITDA is about half a year's earnings. Recomputed from the balance sheet the figure is $13.35B including leases; the difference is definitional and immaterial. Single-A credit rating maintained. |
| "Diversification… happening at pace" | 2025 onward | **Confirmed and now demonstrable.** First-half segment EBITDA: iron ore $6.8B (broadly flat), copper $5.7B (+84%), aluminium and lithium $3.3B (+38%). Iron ore is now under half of group earnings — a genuine structural change, not a slogan. |
| "Medium-term guidance of 345 to 360" million tonnes from the Pilbara | Jul 2024 | **Not delivered on the original terms.** Current Pilbara shipment guidance is 323–338 million tonnes. Greater Nammuldi was flagged as an approvals risk on that very call, and it remains the swing factor. |

**Where the story is richer than the numbers:** the copper cost position, for the gold reason above; and the framing of Simandou as pure growth when a meaningful part of it substitutes for Pilbara tonnes that did not arrive.

**Where the numbers are richer than the story:** margins. First-half gross margin widened to 28.0% from 25.0% on revenue up 14.5%, and the underlying EBITDA margin widened to about 47.8% from 42.9%. Expanding margins on rising revenue is the healthiest combination a resource business can print, and management under-sells it.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rising, with a clear discontinuity at the chief-executive change.**

- *July 2024 (Stausholm):* confident but qualitative. "This is stable, reliable growth." Peter Cunningham, the chief financial officer, is candid where it matters — "Kennecott remains the biggest challenge but also a real opportunity."
- *February 2025 (Stausholm):* defensive framing creeps in. "Our financial results are not the product of a global economy firing on all cylinders." Cost control is presented as a recovery from inflation rather than an offensive lever: "we really feel we have turned the corner."
- *February 2026 (Trott, first result):* an offensive turn, and specificity replaces adjectives. "Rio was entering a new era." Costs are now a programme with a number attached. The Glencore disclosure is volunteered rather than extracted.
- *July 2026 (Trott):* the most confident of the four, and confident in a checkable way. "I told you I'd deliver $650 million in productivity benefits, and we've delivered. We've already banked $870 million." When Glyn Lawcock of Barrenjoey pushes for a multi-year cost-out number, Trott declines cleanly and says why: "the program will mature… inevitably, you start with some of the decisions in front of you." That is a more credible answer than a number would have been.

Safety language moves the other way, and honestly so. Trott opens the July 2026 call with two colleague deaths in the half and says, "Nothing we report today means anything if our people do not go home safely." He opened February 2026 with a fatality at Simandou and announced an independent investigation and an external safety panel. This is a company building the largest greenfield project in its industry and paying for it in lives; the disclosure is not being managed away.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Score: High.**

The record over the reviewed window:

- **Productivity.** Promised $650M by the end of Q1 2026; banked $870M by 30 June 2026; raised the year-end run-rate target to $1.8B. Clear over-delivery, and the individual initiatives are itemised ($80M at Oyu Tolgoi from redesigned underground development, roughly $55M in the Pilbara, roughly $40M across the Atlantic aluminium operations).
- **Dividend.** The stated policy is 40–60% of underlying earnings; the company has paid the top of the range for ten consecutive years. When Alan Spence of BNP Paribas pressed on why the 40% floor exists at all, Cunningham refused to formalise a higher floor — "All I'd say is our policy." That is a deliberate reservation of flexibility, not evasion, and it is the correct answer for a business entering a heavy capital phase.
- **Production.** Copper-equivalent growth of 1% (2024), 8% (2025) and 3% (first half 2026) against an ambition of about 3% compound to 2030 — delivered, with 2025 well ahead.
- **Capital spending.** This is the one place discipline has been tested. Half-year capital expenditure of $4.0B in 2024 became $9.5B for full-year 2024 and is now guided at up to $11B in both 2026 and 2027, easing to $10B in real terms from 2028, with sustaining capital about $4B. That is close to a doubling from the early-2020s base. It is being spent on Tier-1 assets rather than on marginal ounces, and the profile is guided down rather than up — but it is the number to watch, because overspending at the top of a cycle is the sector's defining failure mode.
- **Sandbagging.** No evidence of it. If anything the productivity target was set low and beaten, which is a mild and benign form of the same instinct.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Four themes recur, and management's handling of each is informative.

1. **The dual-listed structure.** Asked repeatedly (July 2024, February 2025) whether the London and Australian listings should be unified, Stausholm gave the same answer twice: about a $5B tax cost, and "you have to sit yourself and think how on Earth can you do this and never get your Australian shareholders to pay a premium." Myles Allsop of UBS pushed for the build-up of the $5B and was refused on the grounds that disclosing tax exposure is "not in the interest of the shareholders." An activist holder, Palliser, forced a shareholder resolution on it. The structure persists, unresolved, and it is a plausible standing reason the shares trade below a sum-of-the-parts value.

2. **The Pilbara replacement mines and heritage approvals.** Lachlan Shaw of UBS and Kaan Peker of RBC both pressed in July 2024 on depletion (about 90 million tonnes to 2028 against about 120 million tonnes of new capacity) and on Greater Nammuldi. Mark Davies conceded plainly: "We're just flagging at this stage it's a risk to Greater Nammuldi." Two years later Pilbara shipment guidance sits below the 345–360 million tonne medium-term band. **The analysts were right and the risk converted.**

3. **Kennecott, the Utah copper operation.** It has been the named problem child on every call: "the biggest challenge" (July 2024), a smelter shutdown and conveyor breakdown (2023), a fatality in early 2026, and a furnace breach in late June 2026 that pushes metal sales into 2027. In July 2026 Rahul Anand of Morgan Stanley asked directly how Rio would de-risk an asset it now expects to grow production 40–50% and to underpin copper beyond 2030. Trott's answer led with safety and optionality rather than with an engineering plan. **This is the pressure point where management is least specific and the stakes are rising.**

4. **Mongolia.** Kate McCutcheon of Bank of America put the tax dispute at roughly $900M in July 2026 and said, fairly, "optically, that's not a great place to be." Cunningham confirmed formal arbitration. Oyu Tolgoi is the single asset carrying the copper growth thesis to 500,000 tonnes a year between 2028 and 2036, and its host government is in arbitration with its operator.

**What analysts are not asking about, and should be:** how much of the copper cost improvement survives a lower gold price, and what Simandou's 60 million tonnes a year does to the iron ore price Rio receives on its other 330 million tonnes.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Concerning**

- Safety has deteriorated during the largest build in company history: a fatality at Simandou in February 2026, two colleague deaths in the first half of 2026. Management's response — stopping site works, an independent investigation, an external advisory panel — is the right one, but the trend is the wrong direction (Feb 2026, Jul 2026).
- The copper unit-cost cut on 15 July 2026 rests substantially on record gold by-product credits. Cost guidance that moves with a metal price is not a cost position.
- Kennecott's operating record is poor and its assigned growth is large (every call reviewed).
- The Mongolian tax dispute, roughly $900M, is in formal arbitration against the operator of the crown-jewel copper ramp (Jul 2026).
- Capital spending has roughly doubled from the early-2020s base to up to $11B a year, during a period when commodity prices are historically high. This is precisely the pattern that has destroyed capital in this sector before.
- The dual-listed structure remains unresolved after activist pressure, and management has ruled out unification on cost grounds without showing the arithmetic (Jul 2024, Feb 2025).
- Pilbara growth guidance quietly stepped down while the group number was maintained with new supply from Guinea (Jul 2024 versus 2026 guidance).

**Positive**

- Productivity over-delivered and the target nearly tripled, with named initiatives rather than a top-down budget cut. Trott: "This is not a top-down exercise where we simply squeeze budgets" (Jul 2026).
- Rio walked away from a merger with Glencore on valuation grounds and said so publicly: "we concluded that we could not reach an agreement that would deliver value for Rio Tinto shareholders" (Feb 2026). Declining a transformative deal is the rarest form of capital discipline.
- The Arcadium lithium acquisition was made near the bottom of the lithium cycle; lithium EBITDA has since quadrupled from a small base and realised prices rose to $18,960 a tonne of lithium carbonate equivalent from $15,580.
- Explicit refusal to be a forced seller of the titanium dioxide and borates businesses: "if we don't get the sort of value that we see in the business, we won't progress them" (Feb 2026).
- The balance sheet absorbed the Arcadium purchase and still sits at about half a year's EBITDA of net debt, with net debt falling in the first half despite $5B of capital spending and $4.2B of dividends paid.
- Diversification is now arithmetic rather than aspiration: more than half of first-half EBITDA came from copper, aluminium and lithium.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

- **The vocabulary swap is the story.** Stausholm's register was moral and institutional — social licence, impeccable environmental and social standards, four objectives. Trott's is industrial and countable — "banked," "run rate," "management operating system," "$870 million." Investors should read the change as a shift in what the board is rewarding.
- **"85% of exploration budget towards copper"** (February 2026) is the most consequential sentence in four calls. Management is telling you, with money, that it does not believe the next decade of value creation is in iron ore.
- **Iron ore's adjective changed.** In 2024 it was the engine. By February 2026 it is "resilient" and "structurally balanced," defended by a steep cost curve and "over 100 price-sensitive producers from more than 20 countries." That is the language of a business being defended, not grown.
- **Cunningham's dividend answer.** Pressed twice to lift the payout floor, he would not. Read alongside up-to-$11B annual capital spending, the message is that the growth programme has first claim on cash and the dividend will grow with earnings, not with the payout ratio.
- **The marketing hint.** Post-Glencore, Trott twice returned to "that marketing front end" and "ways we can generate greater value around those flows." A trading and commercial margin initiative appears to be forming that has not yet been quantified.
- **Simandou's schedule language tightened but its ramp shape never did.** Asked in February 2025 for the ramp profile, Stausholm said, "I'm not able to offer you anything better than a straight line at this point in time without promising you that it is a straight line." Eighteen months later the project is more than three-quarters complete with first high-grade sales in April 2026 and completion targeted for end-2027, but the ramp shape is still unquantified.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.**

The trajectory is genuinely improving on evidence rather than on narrative. A new chief executive set a measurable cost target, beat it, and raised it; the portfolio has diversified away from iron ore in fact and not merely in intention; margins are widening on rising revenue; the balance sheet absorbed a $6.7B acquisition and is still at about half a year's earnings of net debt; and management walked away from a transformative merger on price.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the operations — the price of the things it digs up. Copper is at roughly $6.65 a pound, aluminium realisations at $4,343 a tonne, and gold at roughly $4,152 an ounce, all at or near historic extremes; iron ore at about $93 a tonne is merely normal. The internal torque measure says a 10% move in the commodity basket swings EBITDA by roughly 25%, and a bottom-up check of Rio's own volumes puts it near 20% — either way the swing on a 10% move is roughly $5.5B of EBITDA, and **that arithmetic works identically in both directions**. The shares have risen about 66% from their 52-week low of $59.49 and sit within 12% of their 52-week high. You are being asked to buy a first-quartile cost position at a moment when the prices it earns are not first-quartile normal. Size to the commodity risk, not to the quality of the assets.

**Economic moat: WIDE.** The moat type is scale-cost, and it is real rather than argued. Pilbara unit costs of $23.5–25.0 a tonne sit against a seaborne price of about $93 and a cost curve management describes as supported "at the top end by over 100 price-sensitive producers from more than 20 countries." Sixty years of integrated rail, port and power infrastructure across eight billion tonnes shipped cannot be replicated by a competitor with capital alone; the orebodies and the corridors are not for sale. Copper net unit costs of 30–50 cents a pound are first-quartile even after discounting the gold credit. Returns support the width and are improving, not fading: return on capital employed of about 14% and return on equity of about 19% on the trailing twelve months, with EBITDA margins widening about 490 basis points year on year. That is a widening picture on margins and a stable one on returns, so the trend is best read as **STABLE** — the cost-out is real, but heavier capital spending is temporarily diluting returns while Simandou and Oyu Tolgoi are built and not yet earning.

**Secular threat: material, not terminal.** The named structural force is the erosion of Chinese steel demand — down as much as 30% from its 2020 peak on management's own repeated telling — compounded by Rio adding 60 million tonnes a year of new Guinean supply into that same market. Roughly 46% of first-half EBITDA still comes from iron ore, so this is not a small exposure. But it is a shrinking-market problem rather than a disappearing-market one, and Rio is positioned at the bottom of the cost curve, which is where survivors sit. Set against it, the other half of the business — copper, aluminium and lithium — is levered to electrification, grid build-out and data-centre power demand, which are structural tailwinds rather than headwinds. The cheapness on offer is therefore **not** a value trap; the risk here is cyclical mispricing at the top of a price cycle, not terminal erosion of the earnings base.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STRENGTHENING | MOAT: WIDE | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: material

interrogator_dossier:
# Royal Gold, Inc. (RGLD) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared 4 August 2026. Live price used throughout: $207.27 on the Nasdaq, in US dollars (quote taken 4 August 2026). Gold futures on the same day: $4,153.90 an ounce, against a 200-day average of $4,587 and a 52-week high of $5,626.80.*

Royal Gold is not a mine operator. It owns royalties and streams — contracts that entitle it to a slice of the gold, silver and copper produced at mines other companies build and run. A royalty pays a percentage of revenue with no cost attached. A stream is a prepaid purchase agreement: Royal Gold paid cash years ago and now buys metal at a fixed or heavily discounted price and sells it at the market price. That distinction governs everything below, because it means the company's unit cost is written into a contract rather than dug out of the ground.

Transcripts reviewed: five consecutive quarterly calls from 8 May 2025 through 7 May 2026, plus the company's preliminary second-quarter 2026 disclosure filed 21 July 2026.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

The story changes shape decisively at the midpoint of this window, and management tells you so directly.

**Opening posture (first quarter 2025, 8 May 2025) — a steady, mature royalty book.** The emphasis is on continuity: a "solid start," an adjusted EBITDA margin (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, as a share of revenue) of 82%, and the full repayment of the Rainy River advanced stream deposit, an investment made back in 2015. The new-business ambition is modest and explicitly bounded — chief executive Bill Heissenbuttel tells analyst Tanya Jakusconek that normal deal size is "$100 million to $300 million." The largest single new item that quarter is a $50 million top-up at Xavantina. This is a company describing itself as a compounder, not a consolidator.

**The pivot (second quarter 2025, 7 August 2025) — scale becomes the story.** In one quarter the company announces the acquisitions of Sandstorm Gold and Horizon Copper and buys a $1 billion gold stream on First Quantum's Kansanshi copper mine in Zambia. The language changes with it: Royal Gold is now positioning itself as "a premier growth company," and the specific promise made is diversification — "no asset accounting for more than about 12% of net asset value" once the deals close. Management is careful to frame this as scale, not a change of direction: "these transactions do not shift our strategic focus."

**Execution (third quarter 2025, 7 November 2025).** Sandstorm and Horizon close on 20 October 2025. The first Kansanshi gold delivery arrives in early October. Two pieces of genuinely good operating news land in the same quarter: Centerra extends Mount Milligan's mine life from 2036 to 2045, and Barrick's update on the Fourmile deposit describes a "multigenerational project" with the potential to produce 600,000 to 750,000 ounces a year over 25 years — ground Royal Gold covers with royalties bought in 2022 at an effective 1.6% gross rate.

**Digestion (fourth quarter and full year 2025, 19 February 2026).** 2025 revenue of $1.03 billion, operating cash flow of $705 million, net income of $466 million. Heissenbuttel calls it "a transformational year." The portfolio is now roughly 80 producing and 30 development interests, and the company changes its disclosure to group interests regionally. The dividend rises for the 25th consecutive year, to $1.90 a share.

**Consolidation and, for the first time, self-purchase (first quarter 2026, 7 May 2026).** Revenue of $469 million, up 143% year over year. $300 million repaid on the revolving credit facility. Two new tools announced: a $600 million accordion that would take total revolver capacity to $2 billion, and a $500 million share repurchase authorisation — the first in the company's history. The reasoning Heissenbuttel gives is the single most useful valuation sentence in the entire file, quoted in full in section 7.

The growth driver that was quietly dropped: the standalone development-equity model. Royal Gold spent this window unwinding exactly that. It restructured the Bear Creek debt and equity holdings into cash, Calibre Silver shares and royalties on Corani and Mercedes (first quarter 2026), sold the Highlander shares, and on 18 May 2026 cut its Hod Maden project interest from a joint-venture equity stake to a 15% interest plus a royalty. Each move trades capital-call exposure for contract exposure. That is a narrowing back toward the core model, and it is the right direction.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials

| Management's claim | Where and when | What the numbers say | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Adjusted EBITDA margin held at 82–84% throughout | Every call, 2025–26 | Trailing-twelve-month margin on a reported basis is 78.7% ($1.027 billion on $1.306 billion of revenue). Quarterly reported margins: 83.8% (Q2 2025), 80.2% (Q3 2025), 63.5% (Q4 2025), 87.7% (Q1 2026) | **Holds, with one explained gap.** The 63.5% quarter is the Sandstorm and Horizon transaction charges, which management flagged in advance and promised to isolate. The trailing figure understates the run rate by roughly four points for that reason |
| Unit cost is low and stable | Implied throughout | Confirmed independently: the 21 July 2026 preliminary release puts stream-segment cost of sales at **$871 per gold-equivalent ounce** against a quarterly gold average of **$4,506** | **Verified.** A cash margin near 81% on the stream book alone, with the royalty book carrying essentially no cost of sales |

Gross debt then went to $965.6 million at 31 December 2025 to fund the deals, back to $595.7 million at 31 March 2026, and to **$400 million drawn at 30 June 2026** after a further $200 million repayment | **True, then reversed, then being repaired on schedule.** Management said the money would go to debt repayment and it did |
